name: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
memory_bandwidth_basis: Datasheet spec table prints 'Memory interface 512-bit' and 'Memory bandwidth 1792 GB/s' directly (derived: 28 Gbps GDDR7 x 512-bit / 8). Identical bus and bandwidth to the GeForce RTX 5090, but 3x the capacity and with ECC.
notes:
AUDIT 2026-10-03 (NVIDIA dense/sparse convention re-verified from the primary whitepaper PDF, no values changed): NVIDIA's GeForce RTX Blackwell architecture whitepaper (source consumer-nvidia-rtx-blackwell-gpu-architecture-whitepaper, images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/geforce/blackwell/) prints every tensor row in the form 'DENSE/SPARSE' and defines the second number in a single footnote that is identical on every appendix page: 'Effective TOPS / TFLOPS using the Sparsity Feature'. Every 'Peak ... Tensor TFLOPS' and 'Peak INT8 Tensor TOPS' row on the sheet therefore carries that marker, while the 'non-Tensor' rows (FP32/FP16/BF16 non-tensor, Peak INT32 TOPS non-Tensor) and the RT TFLOPS row do NOT. Each sparse row was re-checked against that sheet page by page and every dense:false row on this record corresponds to a printed second number, with its dense twin present as a separate dense:true row. Note the sheet's own footnote 1, 'Peak rates are based on GPU Boost Clock' - these are boost-clock peaks, not sustained, and not measured. Blackwell workstation part. The distinguishing row is FP4: fp4 4000 stored here as dense:false is the sparse figure, dense being 2000. On Blackwell consumer cards FP4 is the one precision where the dense/sparse pair is printed as 'DENSE/SPARSE' rather than with a separate sparsity marker, so a mechanical reader can pick the wrong column; the whitepaper's GB202 appendix reads 'Peak FP4 Tensor TFLOPS with FP32 Accumulate (FP4 AI TOPS) 1676/3352' on the RTX 5090, i.e. dense-then-sparse for FP4 while every other row on the same page is sparse-marked - the ordering is not consistent even within one table, which is why the per-row basis has to be checked rather than inferred. Workstation part: 24064 CUDA cores, 5th-gen Tensor cores with FP4, 4th-gen RT cores, 600 W total board power, PCIe 5.0 x16, dual slot extended height, 4x DisplayPort 2.1b, double-flow-through cooling. MIG support up to 4x 24 GB / 2x 48 GB / 1x 96 GB - the partitioning is what makes it a multi-tenant single-card option for serving several models in parallel.

PRECISION CAVEAT - this is the most conflated spec on consumer/workstation hardware. The datasheet headline 'delivers up to 4000 TOPS of AI processing power' and the spec row 'AI TOPS 4000' both carry footnotes '1. Peak rates based on GPU Boost Clock' and '2. Effective FP4 TOPS WITH SPARSITY'. So:
  - 4000 TOPS = FP4 with 2:4 structured sparsity (vendor_claim, sparse).
  - Dense FP4 would be ~2000, but NVIDIA does not print a dense FP4 row in this datasheet, so that figure is deliberately NOT recorded rather than derived by halving an unverified marketing number.
  - It is emphatically not FP16/BF16 throughput, and it must not be used as a speedup multiplier for a bf16 or fp8 inference kernel.
PRECISION CAVEAT - the single most conflated number on consumer hardware. NVIDIA's product pages advertise 'AI TOPS' (5090: 3352, 5080: 1801, 5070 Ti: 1406). The RTX Blackwell whitepaper labels the identical figure 'Peak FP4 Tensor TFLOPS with FP32 Accumulate (FP4 AI TOPS) 1676/3352', where the second value uses the 2:4 structured-sparsity feature (footnote 2: 'Effective TOPS / TFLOPS using the Sparsity Feature'). So the marketing 'AI TOPS' number is FP4 with 2:4 sparsity, not INT4, not FP16, and not dense. It is not comparable to an FP16/BF16 dense figure, to the INT4-vs-FP16 speedup ratios quoted in quantization literature, or to another vendor's dense INT8 number. Only figures NVIDIA publishes with an explicit dense/sparse split are recorded here; every flops entry's dense flag states which half it is.

For inference this is the single-GPU capacity leader in this slice: 96 GB ECC GDDR7 at 1792 GB/s - same bandwidth as a 32 GB RTX 5090 with 3x the memory. That is the difference between 'a 13B model in 4-bit with no headroom' and 'a 70B-class model in fp8 with KV cache to spare', in one card. It is also the clearest illustration that capacity and bandwidth are independent: if you need both, you are paying for both.
